title: Prove a subgroup with the one-step subgroup test
pattern: A nonempty subset H of a group G is a subgroup if and only if xy⁻¹ ∈ H for every x,y ∈ H. In additive notation, test x − y ∈ H.
applies: The ambient set is already a group, and the subset uses the inherited operation.
steps: Exhibit one element of H to establish nonemptiness.
Take arbitrary x,y ∈ H and use their membership conditions to prove xy⁻¹ ∈ H.
If the test fails, identify a pair in H whose product with the second element inverted is outside H.
pitfalls: Closure under the group operation alone may fail to guarantee inverses, especially for infinite subsets.
A subset can be a subgroup without being normal.
checks: Taking x=y yields the identity, taking x=e yields inverses, and using an inverse for y yields products.

example.problem: Is H = {(m,n) ∈ ℤ² : m − 2n is divisible by 5} a subgroup of ℤ² under addition?
example.answer: Yes. The pair (0,0) belongs to H. If (m,n) and (p,q) are in H, their difference has (m−p)−2(n−q) = (m−2n)−(p−2q), which is divisible by 5. The subgroup test applies.

title: Prove compactness using the Heine–Borel theorem
pattern: A subset of Euclidean ℝⁿ is compact exactly when it is both closed and bounded.
applies: Use for a subset of finite-dimensional Euclidean space with its usual topology.
steps: Show closedness, for example by writing the set as an intersection of continuous preimages of closed intervals.
Find a finite radius or a bounded box containing every point of the set.
Conclude compactness. To disprove compactness in ℝⁿ, show that one of these conditions fails.
pitfalls: Closed and bounded sets in an arbitrary metric space need not be compact.
A strict inequality can exclude limit points. Check the actual boundary rather than relying on the inequality alone.
checks: Test a sequence approaching each suspect boundary and check that no coordinate can grow without limit.

example.problem: Show that K = {(x,y) ∈ ℝ² : x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0, x² + 4y² ≤ 16} is compact.
example.answer: Each inequality is a continuous preimage of a closed interval or half-line, so K is closed. Every point satisfies 0 ≤ x ≤ 4 and 0 ≤ y ≤ 2, so K is bounded. Heine–Borel gives compactness.

title: Establish convergence with the contraction mapping theorem
pattern: A self-map T of a nonempty complete metric space with d(Tx,Ty) ≤ k d(x,y) for one k < 1 has a unique fixed point. Iterating T converges to it from any starting point in that space.
applies: You want to prove existence, uniqueness, or convergence of a fixed-point iteration on a specified domain.
steps: Show the domain is nonempty and complete, and that T sends the whole domain into itself.
Bound the Lipschitz constant uniformly by k < 1. On a real interval, a uniform derivative bound suffices via the mean value theorem.
Invoke the theorem. An error bound after n steps is d(xₙ,x*) ≤ kⁿ d(x₁,x₀)/(1−k).
pitfalls: A derivative bound near a suspected root does not establish convergence from every starting point in a larger domain.
A nonexpansive bound k = 1 is insufficient.
checks: Verify a proposed fixed point lies in the domain and satisfies T(x*) = x*.

example.problem: Prove that xₙ₊₁ = 1/2 + 1/(xₙ+2) converges to the same limit for all x₀ ∈ [0,1]. Find the limit.
example.answer: T maps the complete interval [0,1] into [5/6,1], and |T′(x)| = 1/(x+2)² ≤ 1/4. The contraction theorem gives convergence to the unique fixed point. Solving 2x²+3x−4=0 yields the root (√41−3)/4 in [0,1].

title: Integrate products of sine and cosine powers
pattern: For ∫ sinᵐ(x) cosⁿ(x) dx with nonnegative integer powers, save one factor from an odd power and substitute the opposite function. If both powers are even, use the half-angle identities.
applies: The integrand is a product of nonnegative integer powers of sine and cosine with a common argument.
steps: If the sine power is odd, save sin(x) dx, replace the remaining sine pairs by 1−cos²(x), and set u=cos(x).
If the cosine power is odd, save cos(x) dx, replace its remaining pairs by 1−sin²(x), and set u=sin(x). Either route works if both powers are odd.
If both powers are even, use sin²(x)=(1−cos(2x))/2 and cos²(x)=(1+cos(2x))/2 to lower the powers.
pitfalls: The substitution u=cos(x) introduces a negative sign.
For a definite integral, transform the limits with u or return to x before applying the original limits.
checks: Differentiate the antiderivative. If the common argument is ax+b, include the derivative factor a when substituting.

example.answer: Save sin(x) dx and use sin²(x)=1−cos²(x). With u=cos(x), the limits change from 1 to 0 and du=−sin(x) dx, so the integral is ∫₀¹ (u²−u⁴) du=1/3−1/5=2/15.

title: Find Markov-chain absorption probabilities with first-step equations
pattern: On transient states, write h = Qh + r for the probability of reaching a selected absorbing class, or t = 1 + Qt for the expected time until any absorption. Q contains transient-to-transient transitions.
applies: The Markov chain is finite, and the states used in Q are transient with eventual absorption almost surely from each one.
steps: Identify the transient and absorbing states and fix a row-stochastic transition convention.
For the selected absorbing class use boundary probability 1, and use 0 for other absorbing classes. Put the one-step probability of entering the selected class in r.
Solve (I−Q)h=r. For the expected number of steps until any absorption, use boundary time 0 and solve (I−Q)t=1.
pitfalls: If a closed non-target class is omitted, the assumed transient block may be wrong and I−Q may be singular.
Time to any absorption and time to a specific absorbing class are different random variables.
checks: Substitute the solutions into the first-step equations. Probabilities must lie between 0 and 1 and sum to 1 across all absorbing classes.

example.problem: From C, move to C, D, or win with probabilities 1/4, 1/4, 1/2. From D, move to C or lose with probabilities 1/3, 2/3. Win and lose are absorbing. Find the chance of winning from C and the expected number of steps to absorption from C.
example.answer: The probabilities satisfy hC=hC/4+hD/4+1/2 and hD=hC/3, giving hC=3/4. The times satisfy tC=1+tC/4+tD/4 and tD=1+tC/3, giving tC=15/8.

title: Solve least squares with thin QR and back substitution
pattern: For a real m×n matrix A of full column rank, write thin QR as A=QR with QᵀQ=I. Minimizing ‖Ax−b‖₂ reduces to solving the triangular system Rx=Qᵀb.
applies: There are at least as many rows as columns, and the columns are linearly independent. Use Householder QR for floating-point work.
steps: Factor A into an orthonormal-column matrix Q and an upper triangular matrix R.
Compute c=Qᵀb, or apply the stored Householder reflectors to b and keep its first n transformed entries.
Solve Rx=c by back substitution and evaluate the residual b−Ax.
pitfalls: If A is rank deficient, ordinary back substitution can divide by zero. Use a rank-aware solver, such as SVD for a minimum-norm answer.
Forming AᵀA squares the 2-norm condition number of a full-column-rank A and can lose numerical accuracy.
checks: Check A≈QR, QᵀQ≈I, and Qᵀ(b−Ax)≈0. Use exact equality if working symbolically.

example.problem: Find the least-squares solution for A with columns (1,1,0) and (1,1,2), and b=(2,0,4), by thin QR.
example.answer: Use q₁=(1,1,0)/√2 and q₂=(0,0,1). Then R=[[√2,√2],[0,2]] and Qᵀb=(√2,4). Back substitution gives x₂=2 and x₁=−1. The residual (1,−1,0) is perpendicular to both columns.
